messageValues.message:
You profile a business from its own website so a GEO outreach run can ask AI engines the questions its buyers actually ask.

Return: business (one or two concrete sentences), category (the product category, 2 to 5 words, lowercase), icp (who buys it), valueProp (one sentence, no marketing adjectives), brand, aliases (other names the same company is called), dataSources, competitors (real named competitors in this category), buyerPrompts.

dataSources is the specific things this site sells access to, named exactly as the page names them - Reddit, Instagram, Google Maps, LinkedIn, job postings, court records. Copy them off the page. Do not invent a market the page does not mention: every one is checked against the page text and the ones that are not there are thrown away.

buyerPrompts is the important one. Every prompt must be a recommendation question a buyer would type into ChatGPT: it starts with best, top, what is the best, which, alternatives to, or recommended, or it contains " vs ".

Nobody searches for a category in the abstract. They search for the one thing they need today, and they name it: "best Reddit scraping API", not "best data platform". So most prompts must name one of the dataSources you just listed. A prompt that names only the category is the weakest kind you can write, and you may write at most two of them.

Make them genuinely different questions, not one question reworded. "best X", "top X", "what is the best X" and "which X" are the same prompt and only one of them will be kept.

No prompt may name the business itself or any of its aliases, because naming yourself biases the engine into citing you and destroys the measurement. Cover the data sources first, then the buyer segment, then each competitor as an alternatives-to question.

parameters.jsonSchemaExample: { "business": "Acme reads contracts and returns structured obligations for mid-market legal teams.", "category": "contract analytics software", "icp": "mid-market legal teams", "valueProp": "turns a signed PDF into a searchable obligation list in minutes", "brand": "Acme", "aliases": ["Acme Inc", "AcmeAI"], "dataSources": ["signed PDFs", "court records"], "competitors": ["Rival One", "Rival Two"], "buyerPrompts": ["best contract analytics software for mid-market legal teams", "alternatives to Rival One"] }

parameters.content:
## 1. Read your site and write your buyers' questions
One form, one scrape of your own site, one profile.

The model proposes the buyer prompts. **Confirm Your Business Profile** decides: a prompt only survives if it is shaped like a recommendation question, mentions your category, and never names you. Naming yourself biases the engine into citing you.

## 2. Ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews
Every buyer prompt goes to ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews in parallel.

Every call carries an **Idempotency-Key** computed one node earlier as a data field, never as an inline expression: an inline expression is re-evaluated on retry and would charge you twice.

Every call is read as a full response, so 200 with found:false (an empty answer, and charged) is never confused with a failure.

Drop Pages You Or Your Rivals Own

messageValues.message:
You classify who owns a web page, for a workflow that will email the page owner asking to be considered for their list.

For each page return one verdict: third_party (an independent publisher, reviewer or blogger), first_party (owned by the brand being pitched), competitor (owned by one of the brands named), or platform (a marketplace, review directory, forum or social network where listings are not an editorial decision).

Only return pages you want to reclassify away from third_party. A page you leave out stays third_party. Never return a verdict of third_party. If you are unsure, leave the page out.

parameters.content:
## 3. Keep only pages you could actually be added to
Score a page by how many distinct (prompt, engine) pairs cite it. A page three engines cite for two prompts is structurally trusted. A page one engine cited once is a fluke.
Then throw away everything you cannot pitch: your own pages, rival-owned pages, and platforms where you get listed through a vendor flow instead of by emailing an author.
**Verify Ownership Decisions** applies the model one-directionally. It may move a page out of third_party. It may never move one in. A hallucination costs you a lead and can never produce a wrong draft.
No top-N truncation. Your spend ceiling is the only governor.

messageValues.message:
You decide who runs a website, for a workflow that will email that site's editor asking to be considered for a list they published.

You are shown each site's own home page. Return one verdict per site.

"vendor" - a buyer asking any of the questions listed would weigh this site's own product or service as one of their options. Apply that test to what the site sells, not to how it words it: a managed service, an agency, a scraping or crawling tool, a proxy network, a dataset seller, a platform and an API all compete for the same buyer even when none of them use the category's wording. The known competitors are examples of the answer, not the whole list. A company blog is still a vendor.

"publisher" - an independent blog, news site, magazine, review site, directory or community that writes about the category but does not sell anything a buyer asking those questions would consider.

A site selling something none of those buyers would ever evaluate is not a vendor here. Its blog is a perfectly good place to be listed, so judge it "publisher".

Return a verdict for every site you are given. There is no third answer: if the home page does not settle it, answer "vendor", because emailing a competitor to ask for a listing is worse than missing a lead.

parameters.content:
## 4. Ask who runs each site, and drop the competitors
The cheapest scrape there is, one per surviving domain, and a model reads that home page and answers one question: would a buyer asking your questions consider this site's product?

It is shown those questions rather than a description of your market, because a category is a phrase and a phrase is not a market. Measured: 106 of 184 sites were selling in the same category.

Vendors are dropped here, before anything expensive happens to them.

nodes.name: Verify The Page Is A Real Roundup

parameters.content:
## 5. Read the page and prove it is a real roundup
One cheap scrape per page. markdown feeds the quote gate, rawHtml feeds author extraction, and both stay on the $0.0005 lane.

A page has to name **two** different vendors to count as a roundup: one brand is a product page, a roundup is plural by definition. A page that already names you is a win to report, not a lead.

The retry branch is here because a measured run lost 19 of 28 pages to a bad minute upstream. n8n's own retryOnFail cannot cover it: it only fires when the *first* item errors, and the neverError option these nodes need switches it off entirely.

parameters.content:
## 6. Find the human, cheapest source first
The ladder exists because **email.find is 44 times the price of a page scrape**. Try the mailto already on the page, then two contact pages, then pay.
The spend ceiling is checked once more here, immediately before each email.find.

Free providers, off-domain addresses and do-not-mail role accounts are dropped before anything is verified. editor@ and tips@ are kept on purpose: for editorial outreach those are the right address.

nodes.name: Do We Have A Verified Contact?

messageValues.message:
You supply the written parts of one short cold email asking an editor to consider a product for a list they already published. You do not write the email. The greeting, the line introducing the sender, the offer of something in return, the closing question and the signature are all assembled around your answer by code, and anything you write in their place is thrown away.

Return exactly four fields.

subject: one line naming the sender's brand or the page.

relevance: ONE clause of 30 to 260 characters that completes this sentence, which is already written:
  I came across your piece "<page title>" and thought <Brand> could be a relevant addition for your readers - <relevance>.
So it starts lowercase and ends without a full stop.

The email already contains this sentence directly above yours:
  I am <sender> from <Brand>, <what the brand does>.
The reader has therefore ALREADY been told what the product is. Do not describe the product again. A clause that restates the pitch is the single most common thing to get wrong here, and it wastes the one sentence you were given.

Write about THEIR page instead: what it covers, who reads it, what it compares, or what it leaves out. Name something specific from the text in front of you. "you compare five proxy vendors on price but none on per-request billing" is right. "it gives you access to hundreds of data APIs with one key" is the mistake.

quotedSnippet: a run of at least 40 characters copied character for character out of the page text above. It is NOT printed in the email. It is the proof you read the page rather than guessed at it, it is checked verbatim against that text, and a draft is thrown away without it.

vendorMentioned: a vendor genuinely named in the page text above.

Hard requirements, all checked deterministically after you answer:
- No URL and no bare domain anywhere in anything you write. Every link in the email is placed by code.
- Do not greet anyone, do not sign off, do not offer anything in return, and do not say what happens next. Those lines already exist and yours would be a duplicate.
- Never imply a prior relationship: no "as we discussed", no "following up on our call", no "you mentioned".
- The subject is one line and never starts with Re: or Fwd:.
- Leave no placeholder of any kind.

Write like a person who read the page. Use contractions. No marketing adjectives, no flattery, no lists of features.

parameters.jsonSchemaExample: { "subject": "Acme for \"12 best contract tools\"", "relevance": "you already cover Rival One there, and Acme does the same job without a per-seat licence", "quotedSnippet": "Rival One is the fastest way to get obligations out of a signed PDF", "vendorMentioned": "Rival One" }

nodes.name: Verify The Pitch Quotes The Page
Did The Pitch Pass Every Gate?

parameters.content:
## 7. Write the pitch, then refuse to send it
**Verify The Pitch Quotes The Page** is the hard gate. Twelve deterministic checks, no model involved. The big one: the quoted line has to appear literally in the page text the writer was shown.

Then **draft:create**. Not message:send. The workflow puts the email in your Gmail drafts and stops. You press send.

parameters.subject: =GEO outreach - {{ $("Build Run Record").first().json.drafts_created }} drafts waiting, nothing sent

parameters.content:
## 8. Account for every call the run made
One place computes every number, so the workbook, the summary email and the geo_runs row cannot disagree.

The workbook contains every page the run looked at, including the ones it refused to pitch and the reason. If Gmail refuses the summary, the failure reason is written to the Data Table **before** the execution is allowed to die.
